title: Half Shiva, half Parvati
hook: a poet bows to a couple joined like a word and its meaning, and a sage learns he can't honor one without the other
carry: Shiva and Shakti: two, and never apart

segments.voice: Yesterday: the goddess is Brahman itself, not a sidekick. The gods asked who are you, and she answered, of the nature of Brahman.

A poet sits down to write a long poem about the kings of Raghu's line, one king after another. And the first thing he writes isn't about any king. It's about a word and its meaning. The poet is Kalidasa, whose Parvati this path met in the forest not long ago. Before he tells a single story, he bows to a couple. Not a king and queen: Shiva and Parvati. And he chooses one picture to say how close they are.
screen: `A LONG POEM OF KINGS.` → `FIRST: A WORD AND ITS MEANING.` → `HE BOWS TO A COUPLE.`

segments.voice: Here is the verse, in paraphrase. Joined like word and meaning, for the sake of understanding word and meaning, I bow to the parents of the world, Parvati and Shiva. A word without meaning is just noise; a meaning needs a word to carry it. Two, and never apart. That's how close the poet says the god and the goddess are. A temple story makes the same point with a body. A sage named Bhringi loved Shiva so single-mindedly that he would circle only Shiva in worship, never Parvati. So, as the story is told, Parvati drew close and became one body with Shiva, half and half. In some tellings Bhringi still tried to squeeze between them. The story's point is plain: you cannot honor one without the other. That shared body is Ardhanarishvara, the lord who is half woman: on one side Shiva, ash and matted hair; on the other Parvati, earring and silk. It's carved in temples to this day. Here's the teaching. In Hindu thought, Shiva and Shakti aren't two gods who happen to be married. Many teachers read them as awareness and power, the still and the moving, neither complete alone. Remember the hymn this path met earlier: without Shakti, Shiva cannot even stir. Today: a Hindu wife is often called ardhangini, the half of the body. Some people hear that and think it makes her half a person. Ardhanarishvara says the opposite. Even God, in this picture, is only whole as two.
screen: `JOINED LIKE WORD AND MEANING.` · `BHRINGI CIRCLES ONLY SHIVA.` · `ONE BODY: HALF SHIVA, HALF PARVATI.` · `STILL AND MOVING, NEITHER ALONE.` · then, large: `TWO, AND NEVER APART.`

segments.voice: Choose one simple word that matters to you, home, mother, peace, a name, and say it once, silently, then watch what arrives with it: a picture, a feeling, a face. Say it again, slowly, and rest wherever the sound and the sense meet. If you pray, you can choose the name of the goddess, or Shiva, or the name you use for God.
Shakti as a philosophy. Kalidasa bows to Parvati and Shiva, the parents of the world, joined like a word and its meaning.
Your line: Shiva and Shakti, two, and never apart. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1088 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: VAK, THE GODDESS WHO SPEAKS.`

howItsDone: The opening verse of Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha is learned by students of Sanskrit and recited as an invocation, and images of Ardhanarishvara, half Shiva and half Parvati, stand in temples dedicated to Shiva.

Raghu.meaning: an ancestor-king whose line the long poem follows

Parvati.meaning: the goddess, Shiva's wife; here a parent of the world

Ardhanarishvara.meaning: Shiva and Parvati shown as one body, half and half

Bhringi.meaning: a sage devoted to Shiva alone, in a temple story

ardhangini.meaning: a wife, as half of one shared body

notes: Raghuvamsha 1.1 paraphrased: vāgarthāv iva saṃpṛktau vāgarthapratipattaye / jagataḥ pitarau vande pārvatīparameśvarau. 'Parameshvara' given as Shiva.
Kalidasa is called only 'a poet of classical Sanskrit' to avoid superlatives and dates.
Ardhanarishvara is not in the cited verse; it is a general description of the image. 'Half woman' for ardha-nārī is a gloss of the name; confirm acceptable under the etymology rule.
howItsDone's claim that Ardhanarishvara images stand in Shiva temples is general; Keeper to confirm.
